title: Japan Overtakes Singapore as India's Top FDI Source With $5.71 Billion in Q1
excerpt: DPIIT data shows Japan invested $5.71 billion in April–June 2026 — nearly 29% of India's total equity FDI and more than it invested in all of FY26 — while US inflows collapsed 76%.
body:
• Japan invested $5.71 billion in India in the April–June 2026 quarter — about 29% of India's total $19.81 billion equity FDI inflows, and more than the $3.74 billion it invested in all of FY26.
  • Japan overtook Singapore ($5.22 billion), Mauritius ($2.31 billion) and the Netherlands ($1.38 billion) to become India's top FDI source, while US inflows collapsed 76% year-on-year to $1.34 billion.
  • The surge is driven by big Japanese financial bets: MUFG Bank's 20% stake in Shriram Finance and SMBC becoming the largest single shareholder in Yes Bank.
  • For NRI investors: the reshuffle signals deepening India–Japan capital ties and a rotation away from US-domiciled capital, which may shift where global funds domiciled for India exposure sit.

Japan has become India's largest source of foreign direct investment, channelling $5.71 billion into the country in the first quarter of FY27 — a single quarter that exceeded the $3.74 billion it invested across the entire previous fiscal year, according to data from the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT).

The figure represents nearly 29% of India's total equity FDI of $19.81 billion in the April–June 2026 quarter, which rose 6% year-on-year from $18.62 billion. Total gross FDI, including reinvested earnings and other capital, jumped 22% to $30.65 billion — a 15-year high, according to analysts.

A reshuffled leaderboard

Japan displaced the traditional top contributors. Singapore ranked second with $5.22 billion, followed by Mauritius ($2.31 billion) and the Netherlands ($1.38 billion). The starkest swing came from the United States, whose inflows collapsed more than 76% year-on-year to $1.34 billion, down from $5.61 billion in the corresponding quarter of FY26.

DPIIT's data does not assign causes, but the divergence is consistent with a broader realignment: Japanese capital is moving decisively into India even as some US-domiciled capital pauses amid trade-negotiation uncertainty and tighter global funding conditions.

What's driving the Japanese surge

The headline number is concentrated in financial services. Tamil Nadu topped the state table with about $5.9 billion in FDI, more than double its $2.7 billion a year earlier — a jump largely attributed to the landmark MUFG Bank investment for a 20% stake in TN-registered Shriram Finance. Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), meanwhile, has become the largest single shareholder in Yes Bank.

At the sector level, services led with roughly $7.04 billion, followed by computer software and hardware at $2.84 billion. Analysts note that banking and insurance alone absorbed about a third of equity inflows, while manufacturing barely moved the needle — a pattern that keeps India's industrial-capital debate alive.

The momentum sits inside a longer commitment: Japan has set a target of investing 10 trillion yen — around Rs 6 lakh crore — in India over a decade, and Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal visited Japan last month to deepen trade and investment ties. Goyal said Japanese firms have already invested about Rs 1 lakh crore toward that target.

Impact and analysis

For Indian markets, the composition shift matters more than the headline. Stable, institutionally driven Japanese financial capital tends to be long-horizon money — the kind that anchors valuations rather than chasing them. The US pullback, conversely, removes a volatile marginal buyer, which may partly explain why Indian equities have leaned more on domestic institutional flows in recent quarters.

For the diaspora, the takeaway is structural. The India–Japan capital corridor is thickening fast: two of India's major private-sector banks now have Japanese anchor shareholders, and the 10-trillion-yen pipeline suggests years of deployment ahead. For NRIs in the US, the 76% drop in American inflows is the warning flag — the capital is not drying up, it is changing nationality.

What's next

The test is durability. One blockbuster quarter driven by two banking deals is a spike; three or four quarters of sustained Japanese deployment would be a trend. Watch the October–December data for whether services-and-finance concentration broadens into manufacturing and energy, and whether US inflows recover as trade talks settle.
